documents.text: Tutorial 3 – Solutions Random Variables & Probability Distributions (Discrete & Continuous) Question 1 The RV X has the distribution: x = -2, -1, 0, 1 with P(x) = 0.4, k, 0.2, 0.3. Find k and the mean value of X. Concept used: For any probability distribution, the probabilities must add up to 1: Sum P(x) = 1. Sum the probabilities and set equal to 1: 0.4 + k + 0.2 + 0.3 = 1 ⇒ 0.9 + k = 1 k = 0.1 Mean (expected value): E(X) = Sum of x·P(x) E(X) = (-2)(0.4) + (-1)(0.1) + (0)(0.2) + (1)(0.3) E(X) = -0.8 - 0.1 + 0 + 0.3 = -0.6 Answer: k = 0.1, and Mean E(X) = -0.6 Question 2 A shipment of 6 television sets contains 2 defective sets. A hotel makes a random purchase of 3 of the sets. Find the probability distribution of X (number of defective sets purchased). Concept used: This is a Hypergeometric distribution problem: we are sampling 3 sets (without replacement) from 6 sets, of which 2 are defective and 4 are good. P(X = x) = C(2,x)·C(4,3-x) / C(6,3).

Concept used: This is a Hypergeometric distribution problem: we are sampling 3 sets (without replacement) from 6 sets, of which 2 are defective and 4 are good. P(X = x) = C(2,x)·C(4,3-x) / C(6,3). Total ways to choose 3 sets out of 6: C(6,3) = 20. X can take values 0, 1, 2 (you cannot get more defectives than exist, i.e at most 2). P(X=0) = C(2,0)·C(4,3) / 20 = (1×4)/20 = 4/20 = 1/5 P(X=1) = C(2,1)·C(4,2) / 20 = (2×6)/20 = 12/20 = 3/5 P(X=2) = C(2,2)·C(4,1) / 20 = (1×4)/20 = 4/20 = 1/5 Check: 1/5 + 3/5 + 1/5 = 1  x 0 1 2 P(x) 1/5 3/5 1/5 Answer: Probability distribution: P(0)=1/5, P(1)=3/5, P(2)=1/5 Question 3 A random variable X may assume 4 values with probabilities (1-3x)/4, (1+x)/4, (1-2x)/4, (1+4x)/4. Find the condition on x so that these values represent the probability distribution of X. Note on the OCR'd text: The original scan of this question was badly garbled by OCR.

Find the condition on x so that these values represent the probability distribution of X. Note on the OCR'd text: The original scan of this question was badly garbled by OCR. This is a standard textbook problem, and the probabilities above are the standard form consistent with the fragments visible in the scan ("...4x", "...2", "...3x" each divided by 4). Concept used: Two conditions must hold for a valid probability distribution: (1) every individual probability must be ≥ 0 (and ≤ 1), and (2) all probabilities must sum to 1.

Concept used: Two conditions must hold for a valid probability distribution: (1) every individual probability must be ≥ 0 (and ≤ 1), and (2) all probabilities must sum to 1. Check the sum first: (1-3x)/4 + (1+x)/4 + (1-2x)/4 + (1+4x)/4 = [(1-3x)+(1+x)+(1-2x)+(1+4x)] / 4 = (4 + 0·x)/4 = 1 So the probabilities always sum to 1, for any value of x — the real restriction comes from requiring each probability to be non-negative. (1-3x)/4 ≥ 0 ⇒ x ≤ 1/3 (1+x)/4 ≥ 0 ⇒ x ≥ -1 (1-2x)/4 ≥ 0 ⇒ x ≤ 1/2 (1+4x)/4 ≥ 0 ⇒ x ≥ -1/4 Taking the intersection of all four conditions (the most restrictive lower and upper bounds): Answer: -1/4 ≤ x ≤ 1/3 Question 4 X takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4 such that 2P(X=1) = 3P(X=2) = P(X=3) = 5P(X=4). Find the probability distribution and cumulative distribution function (CDF) of X. Concept used: Introduce a common constant k for the equal quantities, express every probability in terms of k, then use Sum P(x) = 1 to solve for k. Let 2P(1) = 3P(2) = P(3) = 5P(4) = k.

Concept used: Introduce a common constant k for the equal quantities, express every probability in terms of k, then use Sum P(x) = 1 to solve for k. Let 2P(1) = 3P(2) = P(3) = 5P(4) = k. Then: P(1) = k/2, P(2) = k/3, P(3) = k, P(4) = k/5 Sum to 1: k/2 + k/3 + k + k/5 = 1 Using LCM 30: 15k/30 + 10k/30 + 30k/30 + 6k/30 = 61k/30 = 1 ⇒ k = 30/61 So: P(1) = 15/61, P(2) = 10/61, P(3) = 30/61, P(4) = 6/61 Check: 15+10+30+6 = 61  (out of 61) x 1 2 3 4 P(x) 15/61 10/61 30/61 6/61 F(x) = P(X≤x) 15/61 25/61 55/61 61/61 = 1 Answer: k = 30/61; distribution and CDF as in the table above. Question 5 X: -2,-1,0,1,2,3 with P(x): 0.1, k, 0.2, 2k, 0.3, 3k. (i) Find k (ii) evaluate P(X≥2) and P(-2≤X<2) (iii) find the CDF of X, and evaluate the mean of X.

Question 5 X: -2,-1,0,1,2,3 with P(x): 0.1, k, 0.2, 2k, 0.3, 3k. (i) Find k (ii) evaluate P(X≥2) and P(-2≤X<2) (iii) find the CDF of X, and evaluate the mean of X. Concept used: Same idea as Q1 — use Sum P(x)=1 to find k, then read off probabilities of events directly from the table, build the CDF by accumulating probabilities left to right, and compute the mean as Sum of x·P(x). (i) 0.1 + k + 0.2 + 2k + 0.3 + 3k = 1 ⇒ 0.6 + 6k = 1 ⇒ k = 1/15 ≈ 0.0667 (ii) P(X≥2) = P(2) + P(3) = 0.3 + 3k = 0.3 + 0.2 = 0.5

P(-2≤X<2) = P(-2)+P(-1)+P(0)+P(1) = 0.1 + k + 0.2 + 2k = 0.3 + 3k = 0.5 (iii) CDF F(x) = P(X≤x), built by running totals: x -2 -1 0 1 2 3 P(x) 0.1 0.067 0.2 0.133 0.3 0.2 F(x) 0.1 0.167 0.367 0.5 0.8 1.0 Mean: E(X) = (-2)(0.1)+(-1)(k)+(0)(0.2)+(1)(2k)+(2)(0.3)+(3)(3k) = -0.2 - k + 2k + 0.6 + 9k = 0.4 + 10k = 0.4 + 10/15 = 0.4 + 0.667 ≈ 1.067 (= 16/15) Answer: k = 1/15; P(X≥2)=0.5; P(-2≤X<2)=0.5; CDF as tabulated; Mean = 16/15 ≈ 1.067 Question 6 X: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 with P(x): 0, k, 2k, 2k, 3k, k2, 2k2, 7k2+k. (i) Find k (ii) evaluate P(1.5<X<4.5 | X>2) (iii) find the smallest value of lambda for which P(X≤lambda) > 1/2.

Note on the OCR'd text: The probability values in the scanned table were badly distorted by OCR. This is a well-known standard textbook problem, and the reconstruction above (0, k, 2k, 2k, 3k, k2, 2k2, 7k2+k) is the version consistent with the visible fragments and with the fact that it produces a clean quadratic in k. Concept used: Sum all probabilities to 1; this gives a quadratic equation in k. Reject the root that makes any probability negative. Sum: k + 2k + 2k + 3k + k2 + 2k2 + 7k2 + k = 1 Collecting terms: 10k2 + 9k = 1 ⇒ 10k2 + 9k - 1 = 0 k = [-9 ± sqrt(81+40)] / 20 = [-9 ± 11]/20 ⇒ k = 0.1 or k = -1 (rejected, negative probability) k = 0.1, giving: P(0)=0, P(1)=0.1, P(2)=0.2, P(3)=0.2, P(4)=0.3, P(5)=0.01, P(6)=0.02, P(7)=0.17 (ii) Event {1.5<X<4.5} means X = 2, 3, 4. Event {X>2} means X = 3,4,5,6,7. Their intersection is X = 3, 4.

Event {X>2} means X = 3,4,5,6,7. Their intersection is X = 3, 4. P(1.5<X<4.5 and X>2) = P(3)+P(4) = 0.2+0.3 = 0.5 P(X>2) = P(3)+P(4)+P(5)+P(6)+P(7) = 0.2+0.3+0.01+0.02+0.17 = 0.7 P(1.5<X<4.5 | X>2) = 0.5 / 0.7 = 5/7 ≈ 0.714 (iii) Cumulative sums: F(1)=0.1, F(2)=0.3, F(3)=0.5, F(4)=0.8 ... F(3)=0.5 is not strictly greater than 1/2, but F(4)=0.8 > 1/2. So the smallest lambda with P(X≤lambda) > 1/2 is lambda = 4. Answer: k = 0.1; P(1.5<X<4.5 | X>2) = 5/7 ≈ 0.714; smallest lambda = 4 Question 7 X: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8 with P(x): a, 3a, 5a, 7a, 9a, 11a, 13a, 15a, 17a. Find a, P(X≤3), variance, and the distribution of X. Note on the OCR'd text: The scanned probability for x=6 appeared as "18a", which breaks the arithmetic pattern (odd multiples of a: 1,3,5,7,9,11,13,15,17). This is almost certainly an OCR misread of "13a" — the standard version of this classic problem uses odd coefficients throughout, so that is used below.

This is almost certainly an OCR misread of "13a" — the standard version of this classic problem uses odd coefficients throughout, so that is used below. Concept used: Sum all probabilities to 1 to find a, then use E(X) and E(X2) to get the variance via Var(X) = E(X2) - [E(X)]2. Sum: a(1+3+5+7+9+11+13+15+17) = 81a = 1 ⇒ a = 1/81 P(X≤3) = a(1+3+5+7) = 16a = 16/81 ≈ 0.1975 E(X) = Sum x·P(x) = a[0+3+10+21+36+55+78+105+136] = 444a = 444/81 ≈ 5.481 E(X2) = a[0+3+20+63+144+275+468+735+1088] = 2796a = 2796/81 ≈ 34.519 Var(X) = E(X2) - [E(X)]2 = 34.519 - (5.481)2 = 34.519 - 30.047 ≈ 4.472 x 0 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 P(x) 1/81 3/81 5/81 7/81 9/81 11/81 13/81 15/81 17/81 Answer: a = 1/81; P(X≤3) = 16/81 ≈ 0.198; Variance ≈ 4.472 Question 8 A continuous distribution has density f(x) = kx(2-x), 0 < x < 2. Find k, mean, variance, and the distribution function.

Find k, mean, variance, and the distribution function. Note on the OCR'd text: The scanned expression "kx2 x" is reconstructed as f(x) = kx(2-x), the standard form of this well-known problem (a parabola vanishing at x=0 and x=2). Concept used: For a valid density, the integral of f(x) over its support must equal 1. Mean = integral of x f(x), E(X2) = integral of x2 f(x), Var = E(X2)-[E(X)]2. The distribution function (CDF) is F(x) = integral of f(t) from 0 to x.

Mean = integral of x f(x), E(X2) = integral of x2 f(x), Var = E(X2)-[E(X)]2. The distribution function (CDF) is F(x) = integral of f(t) from 0 to x. Find k: Integral from 0 to 2 of kx(2-x) dx = k · Integral of (2x - x2) dx = k[x2 - x3/3] evaluated 0 to 2 = k(4 - 8/3) = k(4/3) = 1 k = 3/4 Mean: E(X) = Integral (0 to 2) of x·kx(2-x) dx = k · Integral of (2x2-x3) dx = k[2x3/3 - x4/4] (0 to 2) = k(16/3 - 4) = k(4/3) = (3/4)(4/3) = 1 E(X2) = Integral (0 to 2) of x2·kx(2-x) dx = k · Integral of (2x3-x4) dx = k[x4/2 - x5/5] (0 to 2) = k(8 - 32/5) = k(1.6) = 1.2 Variance = E(X2) - [E(X)]2 = 1.2 - 1 = 0.2 (= 1/5) Distribution function: F(x) = Integral (0 to x) of k(2t - t2) dt = k(x2 - x3/3) = (3/4)x2 - x3/4, for 0<x<2 F(x) = 0 for x≤0, and F(x) = 1 for x≥2 Answer: k = 3/4; Mean = 1; Variance = 1/5; F(x) = (3/4)x2 - x3/4 on (0,2) Question 9 A continuous RV X between x=2 and x=5 has density f(x) = k/x. Find P(X<4).

Find P(X<4). Concept used: First determine k from the integral of f(x) equal to 1 over [2,5], then integrate the density from 2 to 4 to get P(X<4). Integral (2 to 5) of k/x dx = k[ln x] (2 to 5) = k(ln5 - ln2) = k·ln(5/2) = 1 k = 1 / ln(2.5) ≈ 1.0913

P(X<4) = Integral (2 to 4) of k/x dx = k(ln4 - ln2) = k·ln2 = ln2 / ln2.5 ≈ 0.6931 / 0.9163 ≈ 0.7564 Answer: k ≈ 1.0913; P(X<4) ≈ 0.756 Question 10 A continuous RV X has density f(x) = kx2 e-x, x > 0. Find k, mean, and variance. Note on the OCR'd text: The scanned expression "kx e" with a superscript is reconstructed as f(x) = kx2 e-x — the standard Gamma(3,1) density used in this classic problem. Concept used: Uses the Gamma integral: Integral (0 to infinity) of xn e-x dx = n! . With n=2 here: Integral of x2 e-x dx = 2! = 2, and higher moments use Integral of xn e-x dx = n! for the appropriate power.

With n=2 here: Integral of x2 e-x dx = 2! = 2, and higher moments use Integral of xn e-x dx = n! for the appropriate power. Find k: Integral (0 to infinity) of kx2 e-x dx = k·2! = 2k = 1 ⇒ k = 1/2 Mean: E(X) = Integral of x·kx2 e-x dx = k · Integral of x3 e-x dx = k·3! = k·6 = (1/2)(6) = 3 E(X2) = Integral of x2·kx2 e-x dx = k · Integral of x4 e-x dx = k·4! = k·24 = (1/2)(24) = 12 Variance = E(X2) - [E(X)]2 = 12 - 9 = 3 Answer: k = 1/2; Mean = 3; Variance = 3 Question 11 A continuous RV X has piecewise density: f(x) = ax for 0≤x<1; f(x) = a for 1≤x<2; f(x) = a(3-x) for 2≤x<3; f(x) = 0 elsewhere. (i) Find a. (ii) Find the CDF of X. Concept used: This is a symmetric "trapezoidal" density made of three linear pieces.

Concept used: This is a symmetric "trapezoidal" density made of three linear pieces. Split the total-probability integral into the three pieces to find a, then integrate piece by piece (carrying forward the running total) to build the CDF. (i) Integral (0 to 1) of ax dx + Integral (1 to 2) of a dx + Integral (2 to 3) of a(3-x) dx = 1 Integral (0 to 1) of ax dx = a/2; Integral (1 to 2) of a dx = a; Integral (2 to 3) of a(3-x) dx = a/2 a/2 + a + a/2 = 2a = 1 ⇒ a = 1/2 (ii) CDF, built piece by piece: For 0≤x<1: F(x) = Integral (0 to x) of at dt = a·x2/2 = x2/4 At x=1: F(1) = 1/4 For 1≤x<2: F(x) = F(1) + Integral (1 to x) of a dt = 1/4 + a(x-1) = 1/4 + (x-1)/2 At x=2: F(2) = 1/4 + 1/2 = 3/4 For 2≤x<3: F(x) = F(2) + Integral (2 to x) of a(3-t) dt = 3/4 + (1/2)[3t - t2/2] (2 to x) = 3/4 + (3x)/2 - x2/4 - 2 At x=3: F(3) = 3/4 + 4.5 - 2.25 - 2 = 1  (confirms total probability is 1) F(x) = 0 for x≤0, and F(x) = 1 for x≥3 Answer: a = 1/2; F(x) = x2/4 on [0,1); F(x) = 1/4+(x-1)/2 on [1,2); F(x) = 3/4+3x/2-x2/4-2 on [2,3); F(x)=0 for x≤0, F(x)=1 for x≥3

General note: The uploaded scan (Tutorial-3.pdf) had OCR distortion in several questions (3, 6, 7, 8, 10), where mathematical symbols, exponents and coefficients did not extract cleanly from the original image/equation objects.

Wherever this happened, the question has been reconstructed to match its standard, widely-used textbook form (these are well-known problems from probability distribution tutorials), and a note has been added above the relevant question. If your original worksheet differs in any coefficient, let me know and the solution can be redone with the exact numbers.
